title: Actions and Controls
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Actions and Controls. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Affordances describe what actions are possible; signifiers communicate where and how to act. Constraints prevent invalid actions; mappings connect a control to its effect. Together they make controls understandable before use.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use labels, shape, placement, state, and feedback to make the action and consequence clear. Preserve familiar patterns where they support recognition. Provide shortcuts for frequent expert work without hiding the primary path. Disabled states should explain what is missing when the person can act to resolve it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Build controls around an action contract
turns.text: What changes when we look at build controls around an action contract?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A control must communicate what can be done, the object it affects, whether it is available, the consequence, and the system response. Visual affordance contributes to this understanding, but so do labels, placement, convention, feedback, and prior experience.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A raised shape does not rescue an ambiguous action; a text link can be clear when its behaviour and destination are conventional.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: All states form one contract: default, hover where relevant, focus, pressed, disabled or unavailable, loading, success, partial success, and failure. Keyboard activation, target size, focus order, repeated submission prevention, latency, and screen-reader name are tested with real content. A component is not complete if only its resting appearance exists.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: deleting a workspace?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The visible “Delete” button is a small part of the interaction. The product must establish scope, affected collaborators, retained data, billing consequence, permissions, authentication, and recovery. A confirmation that merely repeats “Are you sure?” adds friction without improving the decision.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at specify the control contract?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Every control communicates possible action through label, affordance, placement, state, and consequence. Use a button for an action, link for navigation, checkbox for independent choices, radio for one-of-many, and switch for an immediate binary state when that model is true. Visual similarity must not erase semantic difference.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Define default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, success, and error. Prefer explaining why an action is unavailable over an unexplained disabled state. Name actions with the real verb and object, especially before irreversible effects. Ensure target size, keyboard operation, and assistive-technology state.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Test the action inside the task; a locally clear control can remain globally ambiguous.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Bind every control to a clear state transition
turns.text: What changes when we look at bind every control to a clear state transition?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: He checks affordance, signifier, mapping, feedback, target size, focus order, keyboard operation, voice label, and behavior at zoom. Icon-only actions are used only when their meaning is established and the accessible name is explicit. Repeated controls identify their target in context; a screen reader should not encounter six indistinguishable “Select” buttons.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Control quality is tested across latency and failure. Multiple activation must not create duplicate bookings. Progress feedback must not imply completion before the authoritative service confirms it. If an action succeeds backstage after the interface times out, recovery should reveal the durable state. The component is complete only when the full transition is designed.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Control design is policy. What the system lets people do, prevents them doing, or makes difficult expresses trust, risk appetite, and accountability.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Controls should let people answer three questions before acting: What can I do? What will happen if I do it? Can I change or recover from it? Signifiers can be visual, textual, spatial, or behavioural; labels often carry the most reliable meaning.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Mapping matters especially when the action is distant from its effect, as in a toolbar affecting a selected object or a toggle changing a setting elsewhere.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Constraints can prevent unsafe or impossible actions, but unexplained disabled controls create confusion. When someone can resolve the condition, say what is required and provide a route to do it. When a control acts on an object, keep the object and consequence visible.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Provide keyboard operation, focus indication, touch targets, and state feedback as core behaviour rather than edge polish.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Mystery icon: appearance implies an action without a clear label or accessible name. Weak mapping: a control’s effect is remote, delayed, or visually ambiguous. Disabled dead end: the product blocks action without explaining the prerequisite. Shortcut-only power: frequent work is efficient only for people who discover hidden commands.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A control looks like a heading until someone hovers it. Another looks destructive but opens a preview. People should not have to experiment to learn the consequence of a control.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Interaction type sets the overall mode. Controls make that mode actionable. lesson 45 applies this to the highest-friction interaction pattern: forms.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Find a control whose behaviour is unclear before use. What signifier, label, or feedback would reduce the guesswork?
